prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clear, original idea (trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels in the clock transition) with a measured, reproducible result: uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, about two orders of magnitude better than the caesium standard. The achievement has been confirmed by many independent laboratories and national metrology institutes, and clock comparisons are routine. It already serves as a probe of relativistic geodesy, fundamental constants and ultralight dark matter, and a redefinition of the second is under active preparation. Attribution is unusually clean: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium demonstrations, and Ye's group carried the clock to record accuracy, coherence and many-body-limited operation. Four of eight members ranked it first, and the supporting arguments differ in emphasis (metrology, fundamental tests, clean attribution), which is more informative than the vote count itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that lattice clocks can be read as a brilliant application of laser cooling, frequency combs and ultrastable lasers, all recognised in earlier prizes (1997, 2005), and of the trapped-ion clock lineage that was recognised in 2012. A committee that wants a prize for a new physical discovery rather than an instrument could prefer IceCube, which opens a new observational window. There is also a real attribution question: the lattice-clock lineage includes Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and others, and ion-clock pioneers could claim the broader optical-clock achievement. I am also working partly from my own recollection of the priority sequence between the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks, and that has not been verified here.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B018 first as the clearest instrument-driven advance, with a clean principle, broad applications and a natural two-person credit. He treats the prior comb and cooling prizes as not disqualifying.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person credit and on maturity. I would qualify the argument that previous prizes are not disqualifying: the citation should be written around the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting many-atom clock, not around precision spectroscopy in general, so that it does not read as a repeat of 2005. I also think that his framing of the clocks as measurement-limited progress is slightly too instrumental. The case is stronger because the many-atom lattice clock exposed new physics, such as collisional and many-body shifts and spin-exchange effects, which Ye's group then analysed. That connects the prize to physics rather than technique alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B007) first. He argues that a new instrument discovered a new messenger, with a diffuse flux at high significance, early evidence for TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, and that Halzen and Karle give a defensible pair.
responses.response: I take B007 seriously and keep it as my first alternative. The diffuse-flux detection is robust and the instrument concept was original. I rank it below B018 for two reasons. First, the attribution is weaker: the detector is a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA and Baikal preceded it, and I do not think two names can fairly stand for the project in the way two names can for the lattice clock, where the idea and its realisation are traceable to two groups. Second, the sources of most of the flux remain unidentified, so the interpretation is still developing, whereas the clock result is a settled, measured number. If the committee puts a high premium on a discovery of nature, I understand his ordering and could support it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks Cirac and Zoller (B032) first as decisive theorists whose 1995 trapped-ion gate and later simulation proposals defined an experimental field, and argues that a theory-only prize is coherent because ion experiments were recognised in 2012.
responses.response: I respect the clarity of their credit and the field they shaped, and I have kept B032 as a second alternative. I am less sure about the argument that the 2012 prize makes a theory-only prize coherent. That prize honoured the manipulation of single quantum systems; it did not credit the gate proposal or the experimental demonstrations of two-qubit gates by Blatt, Wineland, Monroe and others. Honouring the proposal alone would leave the demonstrations unrecognised, which may look unbalanced. There is also an overlap with B015 through Zoller and Cirac that could split the case. I would like to hear how he would handle that overlap.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B018 first for its concrete, measurable results and applications, and ranks B044 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) second as a major discovery in which a theory prediction was confirmed by experiment.
responses.response: We agree on B018. On B044 I share his admiration for the prediction and its experimental confirmation, but I remain cautious about timing. The superconducting pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are unresolved, and the experimental credit is not settled because Yuan Cao and other moire experimentalists lie outside the supplied names. I would prefer to wait until the interpretation has stabilised before choosing between theory and experiment credit. I would not call it premature for a later year, but it is not my choice this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will want a prize for the discovery-level physics of optical clocks, or will prefer a broader optical-clock citation that would reach ion-clock pioneers and other lattice-clock groups.
Whether the priority between early lattice-clock proposals and the first operating strontium clocks is correctly credited to Katori and Ye; this rests on recollection rather than a verified timeline.
How heavily to weigh the discovery of a new messenger (IceCube) against a measurement-driven advance when the committee compares B007 and B018.
The timing of the redefinition of the second, and whether it should affect the committee's view of when to recognise the clocks.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents collaborations with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato, and training in Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group. None of these is among the credited names for the shortlisted candidates, so no specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile. I note only that I work in the same broad community of atomic physics as the clock and cold-atom candidates (B018, B032, B015), and I have tried to weigh these on the evidence.
